questions.question: Design a library management system. What are the key classes?
questions.interviewer_intent: Standard LLD question testing entity modeling and relationship design
questions.direct_answer: Key entities: Library, Book, BookItem (physical copy), Member, Librarian, BookLending (transaction), Reservation, Fine. Book is the catalog entry; BookItem is the physical copy. A Book can have multiple BookItems.

items: Book: catalog record (ISBN, title, authors, genre) — conceptual
BookItem: physical copy (barcode, current status, location) — physical
Member: borrower with member ID, borrow limit, current checked-out items
BookLending: transaction (who borrowed which copy when)
Reservation: member reserves a book when all copies are checked out
Fine: tracks overdue fines per member

answer_sections.content: The key design insight is separating Book (catalog concept) from BookItem (physical copy). A library has one record for 'Clean Code by Robert Martin' but 5 physical copies. When you checkout, you're checking out a BookItem, not the Book. Each BookItem has a barcode, current status (AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT, RESERVED), and a due date when checked out. The Member entity has a maximum borrow limit and a list of current loans. BookLending is the transaction record — created when a book is checked out, completed when returned. This models the real domain accurately: you can search for a Book, see how many copies are available, and reserve one if all are out.

follow_up_questions: How would you handle the reservation queue when a book is returned?
How do you calculate overdue fines in your design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: Library management is the parking lot problem in disguise — but with one twist that trips up almost every beginner.

beats.text: A library system models catalog records, physical copies, borrowing transactions, and member management. The key insight is that there are two representations of every book.

groups.heading: Book vs BookItem
groups.text: Book is the catalog record — ISBN, title, authors. BookItem is a physical copy — barcode, status (AVAILABLE / CHECKED_OUT / RESERVED), current due date. One Book can have many BookItems.

groups.heading: Member
groups.text: Has a member ID, a borrow limit, and a list of current loans. Can't borrow if they have outstanding fines.

groups.heading: BookLending
groups.text: The transaction record: which BookItem, which Member, checkout date, due date, return date. Created on checkout, updated on return.

groups.heading: Reservation and Fine
groups.text: Reservation holds a FIFO queue of members waiting for a book. Fine tracks overdue fees per member.

beats.text: candidates miss: the Book vs BookItem split. Without it you can't track which physical copy is where, or handle multiple copies of the same title. Always separate the catalog concept from the physical object.

speakable_v2.cap: Book is the catalog entry; BookItem is the physical copy. That one distinction unlocks the whole library design.
followup_handoff: How do you handle the reservation queue when a book is returned?
How do you calculate overdue fines?

questions.question: How do you handle the book reservation system in LLD?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test queue/ordered reservation management — Observer pattern application
questions.direct_answer: Reservation uses a queue per book: when a member reserves, add to Book's reservation queue. When a BookItem is returned, notify the first member in queue. Use Observer pattern: BookItem notifies Book on return, Book processes next reservation.

answer_sections.content: When all copies of a book are checked out, members can join a reservation queue. The queue is on the Book entity. When a BookItem is returned, it notifies the Book. Book checks if there's a reservation — if yes, it processes the reservation: assigns the returned BookItem to the first member in queue and sends them a notification. Observer pattern works naturally here: BookItem is the observable, Book (or ReservationManager) is the observer. The notification to the member (email/SMS) can be an event published to a notification service — keeping the library domain clean and not mixing notification infrastructure into domain classes.

follow_up_questions: How long should a reservation be held before expiring?
What data structure is best for the reservation queue and why?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: The reservation queue is where FIFO fairness meets the Observer pattern — and it's a common LLD deep-dive question.

beats.text: When all copies of a book are checked out, members join a reservation queue. The queue lives on the Book entity. When any BookItem is returned, the queue is processed.

items: Book holds a Queue of Reservation objects — FIFO ensures fairness
When a member reserves, add a new Reservation to the queue
When a BookItem is returned, notify the Book via Observer
Book polls the queue: if someone's waiting, assign the returned BookItem to them
Send the member a notification — but keep notification logic out of the domain class

beats.text: Observer pattern: BookItem is the observable. On return, it calls onBookItemReturned() on the Book. Book processes the head of its reservation queue and fires a ReservationAvailableEvent for the notification service to handle.
non-obvious: keep email and SMS notification logic out of the Book class. Publish an event and let a separate notification service consume it. This keeps your domain model clean and testable.

speakable_v2.cap: Queue on Book for FIFO fairness. Observer to trigger it on return. Fire an event for notifications — don't put email logic in your domain class.

questions.question: How do you model search functionality in the library system?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test Strategy pattern for flexible search criteria
questions.direct_answer: Use the Strategy pattern for search: SearchCriteria interface with implementations for SearchByTitle, SearchByAuthor, SearchByISBN, SearchByGenre. LibraryCatalog.search(SearchCriteria) decouples search from implementation.

answer_sections.content: For search, I use the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with one method: matches(Book). Each search type is a separate implementation: TitleSearchCriteria, AuthorSearchCriteria, ISBNCriteria, GenreCriteria. The catalog's search method takes any SearchCriteria — it doesn't know or care which one. This makes the design open for extension: adding a SearchByPublicationYear requires a new class, no changes to catalog. You can also compose criteria: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')) for multi-field search. This is the Specification pattern used in DDD, and it maps cleanly to database queries if you extend it.

follow_up_questions: How would you add full-text search to the library catalog?
What is the Specification pattern and how does it relate to this design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: Search sounds simple until you need to search by title, author, ISBN, and genre — and combine them. Strategy pattern handles all of that cleanly.

beats.text: Library search uses the Strategy pattern. SearchCriteria is an interface with a single matches(Book) method. Each search type is a separate implementation. The catalog's search method accepts any SearchCriteria.

items: SearchCriteria interface: boolean matches(Book book)
TitleSearchCriteria: checks if title contains the query (case-insensitive)
AuthorSearchCriteria: checks if any author name matches
ISBNSearchCriteria: exact match on ISBN
AndCriteria: composes two criteria — both must match

beats.text: To search for a Java book by Joshua Bloch: new AndCriteria(new TitleCriteria('Java'), new AuthorCriteria('Bloch')). Adding a new search type — like SearchByPublicationYear — is a new class, not a change to LibraryCatalog.
non-obvious: this pattern is called the Specification pattern in Domain-Driven Design. If an interviewer asks about Specification, this is the answer — it's Strategy applied to filtering predicates.

speakable_v2.cap: SearchCriteria interface + one class per search type + composable with AndCriteria. Open for extension, zero changes to the catalog.
followup_handoff: How would you add full-text search?

questions.question: How do you handle fines in the library management system?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test temporal logic and transaction handling in LLD
questions.direct_answer: Calculate fine on return: compare return date to due date. If overdue, fine = overdue days × daily rate. FineCalculator (Strategy) handles the calculation. Member has an outstanding fine balance that must be paid before more borrowing.

answer_sections.content: Fine calculation is straightforward: when a book is returned, compare the return date to the due date on the BookLending record. If return date > due date, calculate overdueDays and multiply by the daily rate. I use a FineCalculator Strategy so the rate and calculation method can change without modifying the checkout process. The Member entity has an outstandingFines balance. A business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books until they pay. The FinePayment creates a transaction record and reduces the balance. Like fee calculation in parking lots, I use BigDecimal for money — double arithmetic has floating-point precision issues that would make accounting incorrect.

follow_up_questions: What if a member disputes a fine — how would you handle that in the design?
Should fines be calculated lazily (on return) or eagerly (each day)?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: Fine calculation looks trivial until you realize fine policies change, currencies round differently, and some days are grace periods.

beats.text: When a book is returned, compare the return date to the due date on the BookLending record. If it's overdue, calculate the fine as overdue days times the daily rate.

items: FineCalculator interface: calculate(BookLending, returnDate) returns BigDecimal
StandardFineCalculator: DAILY_RATE times max(0, overdueDays) — zero if returned on time
Member entity tracks outstandingFines balance
Business rule: members with outstanding fines can't borrow new books

beats.text: FineCalculator is a Strategy: StandardFineCalculator, WeekdayOnlyFineCalculator, or GracePeriodFineCalculator can all plug in without changing the checkout process.

production trap: use BigDecimal for fine amounts — never double. Floating-point rounding errors compound in financial calculations and would make accounting incorrect. This is true for any money calculation in Java.

speakable_v2.cap: FineCalculator as a Strategy, BigDecimal for amounts, outstanding balance on Member with a borrow-block rule. Simple design, production-ready thinking.

questions.question: What are the key design decisions in the library management system?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test ability to articulate and justify design choices
questions.direct_answer: Key decisions: Book vs BookItem separation (catalog vs physical), Queue for reservations (FIFO fairness), Strategy for fines and search (extensibility), Observer for return notifications, Member vs Librarian roles (different permissions).

answer_sections.content: The design decisions I'm most deliberate about: Book vs BookItem — the hardest part for beginners is realizing a library book has two representations. Without this separation, you can't track which physical copy is where or handle multiple copies. Reservation queue as a Queue (FIFO) — because reservation fairness matters: first come, first served. Strategy for FineCalculator — libraries change their fine policies, so this needs to be swappable. Observer for notifications — when a book is available, the right member needs to know; Observer decouples the availability tracking from notification logic. Role separation between Member and Librarian: Librarian can add books, block members, adjust fines; Member can search and borrow. These could be separate classes or role-based permissions.

follow_up_questions: How would you add digital/e-book support to this design?
What would change if the library allowed inter-library loans?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a library management system
speakable_v2.hook: The best way to end any LLD answer is to articulate why you made each design decision — it shows you thought, not just drew.

beats.text: Each key design decision in a library system has a specific reason. Being able to state those reasons is what separates a strong LLD candidate from someone who just lists classes.

groups.heading: Book vs BookItem
groups.text: Without this split you can't track multiple physical copies or show per-copy availability. It's the most important distinction in this design.

groups.heading: Queue for reservations
groups.text: FIFO ensures fairness — first reserved, first served. A List would work but Queue communicates the intent clearly.

groups.heading: Strategy for fines and search
groups.text: Both change independently of the checkout flow. Strategy lets you add new policies or search types without modifying existing classes.

groups.heading: Observer for return notifications
groups.text: Decouples availability tracking from notification delivery. The domain class shouldn't know about email or SMS.

groups.heading: Member vs Librarian roles
groups.text: Different permissions: Librarian adds books, blocks members, adjusts fines. Member searches and borrows. Separate classes or role-based access — either is defensible.

beats.text: non-obvious: interviewers often ask 'why did you use a Queue here instead of a List?' Be ready — the answer is FIFO semantics and intent clarity, not just performance.

speakable_v2.cap: For every class and pattern you introduce, be ready to say the one sentence that justifies it. That fluency is the mark of a strong LLD candidate.
followup_handoff: How would you add e-book support to this design?
What would change for inter-library loans?
